notes.definition: If the concentration of one of the reactants or products in a system at equilibrium is changed, the system is no longer at equilibrium and the concentrations of all the substances change until equilibrium is reached again.
explanation: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so all the concentrations stay constant. If the concentration of just one substance is changed, for example by adding more of a reactant or removing some of a product, the rates are no longer equal. The system is no longer at equilibrium, and the concentrations of all the substances change until the rates are equal again and a new equilibrium is reached.

If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again. Using Le Chatelier's principle, the system counteracts the added reactant by using some of it up. In terms of rates, the higher reactant concentration means more frequent collisions, so the forward reaction speeds up. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up too, until the two rates are equal again.

If the concentration of a product is decreased, for example by removing it from the reaction mixture, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again. The system counteracts the loss by making more product. In industry this idea is used to increase yields: ammonia is removed from the Haber process mixture by cooling it until it condenses, and an excess of a cheaper reactant is used so that more of an expensive reactant is converted into product. Increasing the concentration of a product, or decreasing the concentration of a reactant, has the opposite effect and shifts the position to the left.

The system only partly counteracts the change. If more reactant A is added, some of it reacts, but at the new equilibrium the concentration of A is still higher than it was originally, and the concentration of product is also higher. The new equilibrium has different concentrations from the old one.

Colour changes make these shifts easy to see. Yellow chromate ions and orange dichromate ions are in equilibrium: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. Adding acid increases the concentration of H⁺, so the position shifts right and the solution turns orange. Adding alkali removes H⁺ ions, so the position shifts left and the solution turns yellow. In another example, brown iodine monochloride reacts with green chlorine gas to form yellow iodine trichloride: ICl + Cl₂ ⇌ ICl₃. Adding chlorine gives more yellow solid; removing chlorine makes the solid turn back into brown liquid.
keyFacts: Changing the concentration of any substance means the system is no longer at equilibrium.
The concentrations of all substances then change until a new equilibrium is reached.
Increasing the concentration of a reactant: more products form (shift right).
Decreasing the concentration of a product: more reactants react (shift right).
Increasing the concentration of a product: more reactants form (shift left).
Decreasing the concentration of a reactant: shift left.
The system only partly counteracts the change; the new concentrations differ from the original ones.
Removing a product as it forms (for example condensing ammonia) increases the yield.
Using an excess of a cheap reactant converts more of an expensive reactant into product.
Adding acid to yellow chromate turns it orange (dichromate); adding alkali turns it back to yellow.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of a substance in a given volume of solution or gas mixture.
If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the system responds to counteract the change.
The relative amounts of reactants and products in an equilibrium mixture; it shifts right when more products form.
The state reached after a change, when forward and reverse rates are equal again but with different concentrations from before.
A reactant added in a larger amount than needed, often used to shift the equilibrium position to the right.
The amount of product obtained; it increases when the position of equilibrium shifts to the right.

workedExamples.title: Predicting a colour change
workedExamples.question: Iodine monochloride (brown liquid) reacts with chlorine (green gas) to form iodine trichloride (yellow solid): ICl(l) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ ICl₃(s). More chlorine is passed into the tube. Predict and explain what is observed.
steps: Chlorine is a reactant, so its concentration has increased.
The system counteracts this by using up chlorine: the position shifts right.
More yellow ICl₃ forms and the amount of brown liquid decreases.
workedExamples.answer: More yellow solid forms and there is less brown liquid, because the equilibrium shifts to the right to use up the added chlorine.

workedExamples.title: Calculating new concentrations
workedExamples.question: For A ⇌ B at equilibrium, [A] = 0.40 mol/dm³ and [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³. Extra A is added so that [A] becomes 0.90 mol/dm³. At the new equilibrium [A] = 0.60 mol/dm³. Calculate [B] at the new equilibrium.
steps: [A] decreased from 0.90 to 0.60 mol/dm³, a fall of 0.30 mol/dm³.
The equation is 1:1, so [B] increased by 0.30 mol/dm³.
workedExamples.answer: [B] = 0.90 mol/dm³. Both concentrations are higher than at the original equilibrium.

workedExamples.title: Using reacting ratios
workedExamples.question: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. After extra nitrogen is added, a further 0.60 mol of nitrogen reacts before equilibrium is reached again. How many moles of ammonia are formed and how many moles of hydrogen are used?
workedExamples.answer: 1.20 mol of ammonia formed; 1.80 mol of hydrogen used.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that when more reactant is added, only the product concentration changes.
misconceptions.right: In fact the concentrations of all the substances change until a new equilibrium is reached.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the system uses up all of the added reactant and returns to the original concentrations.
misconceptions.right: In fact the system only partly counteracts the change. The reactant concentration ends up higher than it was originally.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think removing a product makes the reaction stop.
misconceptions.right: In fact removing a product makes more reactants react, so more product forms until equilibrium is reached again.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that adding more reactant increases the yield because the reaction goes faster.
misconceptions.right: In fact the extra product comes from the shift in the position of equilibrium, not just from a faster rate.

realWorld: In the Haber process, ammonia is removed by cooling the gas mixture so it condenses, shifting the equilibrium to make more ammonia; unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.
In the Contact process, excess oxygen (from air) is used with sulfur dioxide so that more of the sulfur dioxide is converted to sulfur trioxide.
Chemists making esters sometimes remove water or use an excess of the cheaper reactant to increase the yield of the ester.
higherTier: All of this subtopic is Higher tier only: predicting and explaining the effect of changing concentration on a system at equilibrium, and interpreting data.
examTips: Use the exact phrases: 'more products will be formed' when a reactant is increased and 'more reactants will react' when a product is decreased.
Always mention that the system counteracts or opposes the change, then state the direction of the shift.
For colour questions, link the colour to the substance whose amount increases (for example orange dichromate).
In data questions, use the reacting ratio from the equation to work out how much each concentration changes.
summary: Changing a concentration means the system is no longer at equilibrium.
All concentrations change until a new equilibrium is reached.
More reactant: more products are formed.
The change is only partly counteracted.
Removing product or using excess reactant increases yield.

flashcards.front: What happens when the concentration of one substance in an equilibrium is changed?
flashcards.back: The system is no longer at equilibrium; all concentrations change until a new equilibrium is reached.

flashcards.front: Effect of increasing the concentration of a reactant?
flashcards.back: More products are formed until equilibrium is reached again (shift right).

flashcards.front: Effect of decreasing the concentration of a product?
flashcards.back: More reactants react until equilibrium is reached again (shift right).

flashcards.front: Effect of increasing the concentration of a product?

flashcards.back: Position shifts left: some products react to reform reactants.

flashcards.front: Does the system return to the original concentrations after a change?
flashcards.back: No. It only partly counteracts the change; the new concentrations are different.

flashcards.front: Why is ammonia removed from the Haber process mixture?
flashcards.back: Lowering the product concentration shifts the equilibrium right, so more ammonia forms.

flashcards.front: Why might an excess of one reactant be used?
flashcards.back: To shift the equilibrium right so more of the other (often expensive) reactant is converted to product.
More H⁺ shifts the position right: solution turns orange (dichromate).
Alkali removes H⁺, shifting the position left: solution turns yellow (chromate).

flashcards.front: ICl + Cl₂ ⇌ ICl₃: effect of adding chlorine?
flashcards.back: More yellow ICl₃ solid forms; less brown liquid.

flashcards.front: Explain in terms of rate why adding reactant gives more product.
flashcards.back: Higher reactant concentration means more frequent collisions, so the forward rate increases until the rates are equal again.

questions.question: The concentration of a reactant in a system at equilibrium is increased. What happens?
markScheme: 1 mark: more products are formed
questions.explanation: The system counteracts the increase by using up some of the extra reactant, forming more products.
options: More products are formed until equilibrium is reached again

questions.question: A product is removed from a system at equilibrium. What happens?
markScheme: 1 mark: more reactants react to form more product
questions.explanation: Lowering a product's concentration shifts the equilibrium to the right, so more reactants react.
options: More reactants react to form more product
The position shifts to the left

questions.question: After the concentration of one substance in an equilibrium mixture is changed, which statement is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: the system is no longer at equilibrium until the concentrations adjust
questions.explanation: Changing one concentration upsets the balance of rates. All concentrations change until a new equilibrium is reached.
options: The system is no longer at equilibrium until the concentrations adjust

questions.question: More of a product is added to a system at equilibrium. In which direction does the position of equilibrium shift?
markScheme: 1 mark: to the left
questions.explanation: The system counteracts the extra product by using some of it up in the reverse reaction, forming more reactants.

questions.question:
Iodine monochloride and chlorine form iodine trichloride: ICl(l, brown) + Cl₂(g, green) ⇌ ICl₃(s, yellow)
More chlorine is added. What is observed?
markScheme: 1 mark: more yellow solid forms
questions.explanation: Adding chlorine (a reactant) shifts the position to the right, so more yellow ICl₃ is made.

questions.question:
Yellow chromate ions and orange dichromate ions are in equilibrium: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O
Dilute acid is added. What colour change is seen?
markScheme: 1 mark: yellow to orange
questions.explanation: Acid increases [H⁺], a reactant, so the position shifts right and more orange dichromate forms.

questions.question:
Sodium hydroxide is added to the orange chromate/dichromate mixture: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O
Why does the solution turn yellow?
markScheme: 1 mark: OH⁻ removes H⁺, so the position shifts left
questions.explanation: Alkali neutralises H⁺, lowering the concentration of a reactant. The system counteracts by reforming H⁺ and chromate, which is yellow.
options: Hydroxide ions add more H⁺ ions
Hydroxide ions react with H⁺ ions, lowering [H⁺], so the position shifts left

questions.question: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ammonia is removed from the mixture by cooling it so that it condenses. What is the effect on the equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: position shifts right, more ammonia is made
questions.explanation: Removing a product lowers its concentration. More nitrogen and hydrogen react to replace it.
options: Position shifts left, less ammonia is made
No effect, because ammonia is a product
Position shifts right, more ammonia is made

questions.question: A ⇌ B is at equilibrium. Extra A is added and a new equilibrium is reached. How does the new concentration of A compare with its values before and just after the addition?
markScheme: 1 mark: higher than before, lower than just after
questions.explanation: The system uses up some of the added A, but only partly counteracts the change, so [A] stays above its original value.
options: Higher than before the addition, but lower than just after the addition
Exactly the same as before the addition
Higher than just after the addition

questions.question:
Ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid: ethanol + ethanoic acid ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water
Which change would increase the amount of ethyl ethanoate at equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: adding more ethanoic acid
questions.explanation: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the position to the right. Adding water (a product) or removing ethanol (a reactant) would shift it left.

questions.question: A manufacturer uses an excess of a cheap reactant X in the reaction X + Y ⇌ Z. Y is expensive. What is the main reason?
markScheme: 1 mark: shift equilibrium right so more Y is converted
questions.explanation: A high concentration of X shifts the position to the right, so a greater proportion of the expensive reactant Y is turned into product. The reverse reaction does not stop.
options: To shift the equilibrium right so that more of Y is converted into Z
To stop the reverse reaction completely

questions.question:
For the reaction A ⇌ B, at equilibrium [A] = 0.40 mol/dm³ and [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³. Extra A is added so that [A] becomes 0.90 mol/dm³. At the new equilibrium, [A] = 0.60 mol/dm³.
Calculate [B] at the new equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: [A] fell by 0.90 − 0.60 = 0.30 mol/dm³, so [B] rose by 0.30 mol/dm³
questions.explanation: The equation is 1:1, so every mole of A that reacts forms one mole of B. [A] fell by 0.30, so [B] increased by 0.30 to 0.90 mol/dm³.

questions.question:
For the reaction A ⇌ B, at equilibrium [A] = 0.40 mol/dm³ and [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³. Extra A is added so that [A] becomes 0.90 mol/dm³. At the new equilibrium, [A] = 0.60 mol/dm³.
By how much did the concentration of A fall after the extra A was added?
questions.explanation: The concentration of A fell from 0.90 mol/dm³ (just after adding) to 0.60 mol/dm³ (new equilibrium), a fall of 0.30 mol/dm³.

questions.question: Using the same data, 0.50 mol/dm³ of extra A was added (from 0.40 to 0.90 mol/dm³). Calculate the percentage of the added A that was converted into B.
markScheme: 1 mark: 60%
questions.explanation: 0.30 mol/dm³ of A reacted out of 0.50 mol/dm³ added: 0.30 ÷ 0.50 × 100 = 60%. The remaining 40% of the added A stays unreacted, showing the change is only partly counteracted.

questions.question:
In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. After extra hydrogen is added, a further 0.45 mol of nitrogen reacts before a new equilibrium is reached.
How many moles of ammonia are formed?
questions.explanation: The ratio N₂ : NH₃ is 1 : 2, so 0.45 mol of N₂ forms 0.90 mol of NH₃.

questions.question: In the same reaction, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, how many moles of hydrogen react when 0.45 mol of nitrogen reacts?
questions.explanation: The ratio N₂ : H₂ is 1 : 3, so 0.45 × 3 = 1.35 mol of hydrogen reacts. Check: 1.35 ÷ 0.45 = 3.

questions.question: A system is at equilibrium. Describe what happens to the amount of product when the concentration of a reactant is increased.
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of product increases / more products form
1 mark: until equilibrium is reached again (position shifts right)
questions.explanation: The system counteracts the extra reactant by converting some of it into product.

questions.question: State what happens to a system at equilibrium when the concentration of a product is decreased.
markScheme: 1 mark: more reactants react (to form more product) until equilibrium is reached again
questions.explanation: This is the exact wording in the specification and replaces the product that was removed.

questions.question:
The tube containing ICl(l) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ ICl₃(s) is opened and turned upside down so that some chlorine gas escapes.
Predict what is observed and explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: yellow solid decreases / more brown liquid forms
1 mark: removing chlorine (a reactant) shifts the position to the left
questions.explanation: Lowering the chlorine concentration makes the system replace chlorine by the reverse reaction, which converts ICl₃ back into ICl and Cl₂.

questions.question:
Yellow chromate and orange dichromate are in equilibrium: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O
Explain why adding dilute sulfuric acid turns a yellow chromate solution orange.
markScheme: 1 mark: acid increases the concentration of H⁺ ions (a reactant)
1 mark: position shifts right, forming more (orange) dichromate
questions.explanation: The system uses up some of the added H⁺ ions by forming more dichromate.

questions.question: Explain why ammonia is removed from the reaction mixture in the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
markScheme: 1 mark: lowers the concentration of the product
1 mark: so the equilibrium shifts right and more nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia
questions.explanation: Removing product means the reverse reaction slows, so more product forms overall.

questions.question: Explain why using an excess of a cheap reactant can increase the amount of product obtained from an expensive reactant in a reversible reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: higher concentration of the cheap reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right
1 mark: so more of the expensive reactant is converted into product
questions.explanation: This makes the best use of the expensive material, even though some of the cheap reactant is left unreacted.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, why increasing the concentration of a reactant leads to a new equilibrium with more product.
markScheme: 1 mark: more reactant particles so more frequent collisions; forward rate increases (becomes faster than reverse)
1 mark: more product forms, so the reverse rate increases
1 mark: rates become equal again at a new equilibrium with more product
questions.explanation: The change temporarily makes the forward reaction faster than the reverse. The gap closes as products build up.

questions.question:
Ethanol + ethanoic acid ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water
A chemist adds a drying agent that removes water as it forms. Predict and explain the effect on the yield of ethyl ethanoate.
markScheme: 1 mark: yield of ethyl ethanoate increases
1 mark: removing water (a product) shifts the position to the right
questions.explanation: Lowering a product concentration makes more reactants react, forming more ester.

questions.question:
For A ⇌ B, a student adds extra A to an equilibrium mixture. They claim that at the new equilibrium, [A] will be the same as it was originally.
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: the system only partly counteracts the change / not all the added A reacts
1 mark: so [A] at the new equilibrium is higher than originally (and [B] is also higher)
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle says the system counteracts the change, not that it cancels it completely.
acceptedAnswers: not all the added A reacts

questions.question:
Iodine monochloride is a brown liquid. It reacts with green chlorine gas to form yellow iodine trichloride crystals:
ICl(l) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ ICl₃(s)
The mixture is at equilibrium in a sealed U-tube. Describe and explain what would be observed if (a) more chlorine is added and (b) some chlorine is removed.
markScheme: Indicative content: (a) adding chlorine increases the concentration of a reactant; by Le Chatelier's principle the system counteracts the change by using up chlorine; position shifts right; more yellow crystals of ICl₃ form; the amount of brown liquid decreases; green colour of gas fades; (b) removing chlorine decreases the concentration of a reactant; the system counteracts by producing chlorine; position shifts left; yellow crystals decrease; more brown liquid forms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct observations for both changes, each explained using the direction of shift and Le Chatelier's principle.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct observation or explanation for one change, or observations without explanation.
questions.explanation: For each change, identify whether a reactant or product changes, state the direction of shift, then link this to the colours.

questions.question:
For the reaction A ⇌ B, these concentrations were measured:
Original equilibrium: [A] = 0.40 mol/dm³, [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³
Just after adding A: [A] = 0.90 mol/dm³, [B] = 0.60 mol/dm³
New equilibrium: [A] = 0.60 mol/dm³, [B] = 0.90 mol/dm³
Use the data to explain how the system responded to the addition of A.
markScheme: Indicative content: adding A increased its concentration from 0.40 to 0.90 mol/dm³; the system was no longer at equilibrium; by Le Chatelier's principle it counteracted the change by using up some A; [A] fell by 0.30 to 0.60 mol/dm³; [B] rose by 0.30 to 0.90 mol/dm³, matching the 1:1 ratio; so the position shifted right; more product formed; the change was only partly counteracted because [A] at the new equilibrium (0.60) is still higher than originally (0.40); forward rate increased at first, then rates became equal again.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses the data accurately to show the shift to the right and that the change is only partly counteracted, linked to Le Chatelier's principle.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies that more B formed or that A decreased, with limited use of data.
questions.explanation: Quote values from the data and link the changes to the 1:1 ratio and Le Chatelier's principle.

questions.question:
Chromate ions (yellow) and dichromate ions (orange) are in equilibrium in solution:
2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
A student adds dilute acid to a yellow solution of chromate ions, then adds sodium hydroxide solution until it is in excess.
Explain the colour changes seen. Use Le Chatelier's principle and ideas about concentration in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: the solution starts yellow because chromate is the main species; adding acid increases the concentration of H⁺ ions, a reactant; the system is no longer at equilibrium; the system responds to counteract the change by using up H⁺; position shifts right; more dichromate forms; the solution turns orange; adding sodium hydroxide: hydroxide ions react with (neutralise) H⁺ ions; this decreases the concentration of H⁺; the system counteracts by producing more H⁺; position shifts left; dichromate reacts with water to reform chromate; the solution turns yellow again; this shows the reaction is reversible and the position depends on concentration; the concentrations of all species change until a new equilibrium is reached each time.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): both colour changes fully explained, linking the change in [H⁺] to the direction of shift using Le Chatelier's principle, with the role of hydroxide ions clear.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both colour changes described with an explanation for at least one, or one fully explained.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or both colour changes stated with little or no explanation.
questions.explanation: The key step for the alkali is that OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ ions, lowering the concentration of a reactant.
